author: buchanan_robert
text: To make our lives sublime, And, departing, leave behind us Footprints on the sands of time;

author: cushag
text:
If we were all but what we ought to be,
How different would our lives appear!
We should not see the sun so often,
For we might lie down on beds of flowers,
Or sit under shady trees that grow
In quiet gardens where no care can go,
Nor any burden press us down
But happiness.

She sat and waited till the dawn would break,
The daybreak when they go forth from their house-door—
Then went out into the moonlight night,
To walk alone beneath the stars that shone.
She met no one on the road, and all were silent.
Yet seemed some strange sound, so near, or far,
So close behind her steps, that made her look,
Though every bush was dark against the sky.
Her heart beat fast, for she was very young,
But still there came no sight nor sound before her,
Save only now

author: buchanan_robert
text:
The girl stood up from where she knelt before the mirror,

Her head high, her hands upon her hips, and smiled;

She had come from school that day, I thought, all weary—
But now she would not take one step back from me,
Until I gave my hand in marriage, till I swore

That my life should be like hers,—that I loved her!

author: buchanan_robert
text:
For he had a wife—a very beautiful woman,

Whom he loved as none but husbands know how

To love. And when from far off they heard the thunder
Of the battle, and knew that their own dear city

author: cushag
text:
Me mother's as white as snow,
An' me father's dark like the night;
I look upon the world as black as coal,
And 't ain't worth the trouble to fight.

author: emily_dickinson
text:
One mornin' early before day-break
I woke up from my sleep;
An' 'tis then that I thought to myself,
That there wasn't no harm in it.

author: cushag
text:
It all comes to the mother-wit,

You know, you've heard it said.

" The wife that has the wit can make a man out o' any old cuss ;

The wife that doesn't may marry two or three before she finds one."

author: cushag
text:
My poor wife! she lies in her grave;
The cold ground is over her now,
An' the stars shine bright upon it above.

But ah! the chudren they linger around,

All about the cottage door ;

" Come back, come back, dear mother!" say,

" For you ne'er did wrong to any one."

author: emily_dickinson
john_keats
text:
I never was so happy as when
   Upon a summer day;
 When from beneath our shady bough
 The warm wind came to me.

And he had a son, whose name was Jack:

What is it to be a boy?
  How fine to play!
 How nice to run and jump and shout,
 With your father and your mother, too!

O let me give you what is mine, 
And all your loss repay;
 For, though so poor this offering be,
 It does not cost a day.

author: emily_dickinson
text:
Behold a man at play;
The world before him lay;
He did not think that day
Would ever come away.
He saw his house and home,
And all he had beloved,
But little thought it none
That this was ever proved.

What is most striking about these poems?

author: emily_dickinson
john_keats
text:
What is it but a world?
Wherein thy eye alone can see what thou wouldst have seen,
All things else being equally invisible;
If not more so, because they are more common,
More in number than thy sight; which therefore hath
A greater power over these, by reason of their multitude.

In this second passage, the author uses metaphors to give us mental pictures. The first part compares life on earth to an "oily" painting or a "dark cloud". We might feel sorry for people who live under dark clouds because they cannot go outside without protection

author: john_masefield
text: The last thing I want is an old man saying ‘Things were different in my day’ — it just shows you have no idea how good things are today compared to when they used to say that sort of stuff.

text: "If I have not done anything for my country, it is because no one has been able to send me there."

author: kemp_harry_1883_1960
text:

His clothes were blowing in the wind and his hair was streaming out behind him
He stopped before me as though he had never moved at all,
But when I looked into his face it wasn't any longer that of a man but of an old child."

author: john_masefield
text:
"But I am young and cannot die;
We know not where, or when, or why."

author: john_masefield
text: "The first thing I did when he came back from his holiday was to ask him why it had been so short a one. 'Because my mother is in such bad health,' he said, 'that she cannot stay out as long as some other people can.'"

author: kemp_harry_1883_1960
text:
God gave us eyes so we may see His light;
He gave our ears to hear Him speak.

My mother’s face is as my mirror, where
I gaze upon myself each day.

Her gentle words remind me always that
Love is not just a word in vain.

author: newman_john_henry_1801_1890

text:
I am tired. . .(and) it is not enough to
die. . ..

My heart has ceased to beat, yet my body goes
on working,

The sea holds me in its grip as if I were still
alive;

It draws the life-blood from my veins; all hope
is over.

Still another poem:

O my beloved child,

Your name shall live on in history.

When the world ends—when all things are destroyed
by fire,

Then, also, when you are dead

In this new world, let my name

author: kemp_harry_1883_1960
text:
Why is this so? Why should one wish to die
so young, while all about are dying in their

prime, with strength and hope still alive within them?

I shall never have children; my heart is not

tender nor sweet enough, though once I tried,

and failed, with anguish, pity, shame.

author: kemp_harry_1883_1960
text:
The Old Lady says she will be in her grave before
I am, so it seems no good trying to live forever,
It might make the world too crowded.

author: newman_john_henry_1801_1890
text: Who will buy for money such as mine to-day?

author: robert_frost
text:
What is the cause of these strange diseases?

The foul air that in me lives; I cannot breathe it.

And another:

Wherefore doth the sun shine as bright on me
As if I had been clad in pure white wool?

I have suffered much from hunger and thirst; I have
been wounded in battle for liberty's sake, but never
have tasted the sweetness of peace before; not even when
the sun rose upon me from behind yon mountain.*

The following is an extract from another poem:

"We did not know what to say or where to go," said one,
while the other replied, "It seems as if we had been
driven out into the wilderness." And now they sat down
to eat their meal. They had brought no food with them
when they set out from home

author: newman_john_henry_1801_1890
text:
I had but little to eat in this prison;
But much I endured of Philip’s cruelty.

author: newman_john_henry_1801_1890
text:
I had rather have been born in a barn

With good horse-fodder than to have been wellborn.

author: robert_frost
text:
"You have been in Ireland quite often, sir?

Yes, but only as a tourist; you are more intimate?"

Well, now, my dear friend, do you know me?

Is this not the old man who used to be our miller?

Ay, ay! We never forget faces or voices here.

author: stephen_crane
text:
“At last we have our man in full dress!
The Lord knows how you sweat on these hot days!
Don't think yourself so very much alone;
You may count all men your brothers. The poor
Man's hard life has made me so. To-day
We'll get a bit more work out of him than
Yesterday, since he needs the money more.”

‘One who’s been on the tramp for years,’ says my companion—not altogether without cause, ‘can always tell another by the way he carries his clothes.’

author: robert_frost
text:
"A beggar sat before me on a log.
The sun shone down upon his shrivelled face;
His clothes were all in rags. His eyes looked cold
And hollow. He had nothing but his stick—
Nothing more than sticks, or stones you might say.
No hope, no faith, no courage left within,
Not even strength enough to stir, except
To seek some shelter for the night awhile.
Poor fellow! I thought how miserable
He must have been, such want of everything.
But still his face would not look sad or dull
With

author: robert_frost
text:
"Once in May, when all things spring again,
On the hillside we were talking this over.
We got no answer then—we saw her face
As pale as death, but just a moment later
Her mother came out from round the corner,
She had been watching us; she turned away
And went into the cottage without speaking.
That evening my wife said nothing whatever.

author: stephen_crane
text:
Two brothers went out one day,
 And on the road they met a wayward girl;
 She cried as she stood there; her hair was wet with tears.
 The boys took pity on her and helped her home.

One brother stayed at home, but the other set off again.
 He ran into another wayward lass who gave birth to twins.
 Her name was Sorrow; it filled his heart with sorrow too.

author: stothert_james_a

text:
The sun was shining
 The leaves were rustling;
 There came a tiny creature
 From under a bush!
 He was so short and small
 That his head was hidden
 By the base of the rosebush
 Which grew beside it.
 And what a queer appearance
 His face had, with its large eyes,
 And its nose and mouth
 Like two dark peas on a string!

author: stephen_crane
text: Two young sisters once upon a time Were sitting side by side; One was named Nancy and one was May. Their mother had gone out to play. The house was empty as they could see. So happy, so joyful and free! And yet the two little girls felt sad, Because they knew not where their mother was; For she would come home from her work at last, If not within an hour or two. But when the clock struck twelve Both the girls went to sleep. Questions 1. How many people

author: stephen_crane
text:
Two crows on top of a tree
 Were talking, and saying, "How fine it is up here!"
 Suddenly they heard some one coming down below;
 And there was a gentleman passing along the road,
 Who smiled at them as he went.

author: stothert_james_a
text:
Forth with the fire of life's bright dawn hath rolled
The day, and now is evening's quiet hour ;

O 'midst a thousand sights that round me roll,
This one alone my soul doth hold most dear :

author: thomas_hardy
text:
How lovely are thy robes, O Muse ! which clothe

The universe, and deck her every part !
Forth from their sources in Thy pure breast they flow

O life and death, how near you lie !

The breath, but just before I die,

Shall draw a little further away.

This little farther space between us we'll stay.

author: stothert_james_a
text:
This day I met a soul-force quite apart,
One like whose magnetism can not be found;
In this short time her touch has made my heart,
And moved me into something new and bound.

I think she's worth remembering, for my sake,
Though when you see her next you will not know,
For we shall both forget the other lake
Of feeling stirred beneath an old face now.

author: stothert_james_a
text:
O Nature! Mother of my birth and life,

Why dost thou ever, through thy varying moods,

So strangely seem to mock me? From her light
I learn to look on thee with scornful eyes,

Nor dare to think that thou canst be my guide ;

But still I turn for help to thee when need
Of comfort stirs within me—and so soon
As that again I seek to trust in Thee,

author: thomas_hardy
text:
The sun sinks low and cold—
 The west is bright and fair!
 I see before me gold,
 The glory of the air!
 It wraps my spirit round
 With loveliness divine,
 As if its light were sound
 That fills my being with delight.

 Oh, never was so fair!

author: william_wordsworth
text:
THE moon hung on her sphere
 Of cold and silence long,
 Until one day she heard
 An answering cry among
 The stars which all around were dark,
 Save where a certain star shone bright.

 Then she arose from rest
 With heart aglow full strong,
 For she had heard a guest
 Who never comes among
 Her kindred stars till now alone,
 And they could not the wanderer long.

THEY sang aloud, they played:
 No word was spoken!  They told
 Of mirth and love, of toil and pain,
 Through glances that could not be mistaken:
 The old were young, the weak were strong,
 The sad felt joy, the weary danced!

author: thomas_hardy
text:
THOUGHTS wander far and wide
 Along the world’s broad way,—
 But those who tread it find
 That not a single thought is strayed!
 For he who travels well must take
 His trammels on his brain away.

author: thomas_hardy
text:
I dreamed I was very young,
In some great city long ago,
And found my way into the park
That borders on a distant lake.
The grass looked greener than it is
And the trees had not yet begun
To tell what life can teach them all,
Nor lost the youth that once they owned.
There were old friends who came along,
Who lived but only half their lives,
Whose hair was white as milk was white,
When first it was just out of wives!

author: william_wordsworth
text: The following lines were written about thirty years ago, in consequence of an incident which took place at Cheltenham. The young lady then living with me had been sent into the town for provisions and some other articles, when she fell in with two women who pretended to have seen her mother dead-drunk in the streets. She was so alarmed by this report that she immediately ran back home and gave it out that she had been murdered. Her father hastened down to town accordingly, but finding no truth in what his daughter had related, he wrote to the magistrates to take charge of her until such time as they could

author: buchanan_robert
text:
I have been watching all day long
 The stars upon their courses roll,
 And the clear moon in the sky-blue night
 To me has come like an angel bright.

Thou art not old, thou art not weak,
   My Star, but young, and strong, and bright!
 Thou hast no years nor wrinkles on thy cheek,
    But like a virgin lookest through thy light!
 Thy head in heaven doth never grow grey;
  The Sun shines down upon thy hair,
 And makes its silver beams more glary:
  And when he sets, it gives his fire away.

author: william_wordsworth
text:
Whence then this anguish, which o'erwhelmeth me? 
  Whence these wild exclamations from my heart?
 Wherefore this fierce tempest from within? 


Wherefore this strife in my breast? This dread of fate?
 Why doth the soul so fiercely yearn to part
 With such a body as mine hath been? - Ah! why
 Doth Heaven send forth from its golden throng
 Such an enchanter of all human joy,
 A being half divine, whom none but she
 Hath ever loved, or can love, since thou art

author: william_wordsworth
text:
O thou whose golden hair is streaked with gray,
 O thou whose restless eyes are wet with tears,
 My heart within me weeps for thee away,
 And all my soul is sad and sore for fears.
 Now hast thou wander'd far from home and friends,
 To where the cold winds whistle o'er their way
 In search of treasure that shall make thee blest—
 That land so fair beyond the western seas!
 Where dwells the people of thy kindred race,
 Whose faces thou would'st greet again in bliss,
